title: International bonds: currency risk
subtitle: International bonds
openingQuestion: A Vietnamese investor buys US government bonds in USD, with a 4%/year coupon. If the USD loses 5% of its value against VND that year, what happens to this person's actual return once converted back to VND?
openingOptions: Still exactly 4% profit for certain, because the bond's coupon rate was fixed from the start and never changes
Much lower, even negative, because the USD lost 5% of its value
The return will rise even higher, because the USD is always stronger than VND in every phase of the economy
There's no effect at all, because US government bonds are always considered absolutely safe under any circumstance
explanation: When investing in bonds denominated in a foreign currency, your actual return (measured in your home currency) depends on BOTH the coupon rate AND the exchange-rate movement. If the foreign currency loses more value than the interest received, you can end up with a net loss even though the bond itself is very safe on a credit basis.

diagram.label: Buy a bond denominated in a foreign currency
Receive the coupon in that currency
Convert to home currency at the rate at that time
If the currency falls more than the interest earned, you still lose even without a default

realWorldExample.company: US Government Bonds (US Treasuries) and USD/VND exchange-rate swings
realWorldExample.description: Many Vietnamese investors with international brokerage accounts are interested in US Treasuries, seen as one of the safest assets in the world. However, the USD/VND exchange rate moves year to year - some periods see the USD strengthen against VND (favoring USD-asset holders), and other periods see the reverse. An investor who buys a US bond paying 4%/year, if VND strengthens sharply against USD during the holding period, will find that converting the return back to VND for spending at home can 'erode' that 4% interest or even turn it into a loss because of an unfavorable exchange rate.

quiz.question: What is currency risk in international bond investing?
options: The risk that an international bond always carries a lower rate than a domestic one
The risk of being unable to resell the bond on the secondary market, something easy to get backwards at first
The risk that the converted return is affected by exchange-rate movement
The risk of a bond's price falling because domestic interest rates rise
quiz.explanation: Currency risk is a separate risk, distinct from the issuer's credit risk. Even a US government bond - nearly absolutely safe in terms of repayment ability - can still deliver a negative return to a Vietnamese investor if the exchange rate moves unfavorably enough.

quiz.question: If you're a Vietnamese investor who believes VND will weaken sharply against USD over the next few years, what benefit could holding part of your assets in USD bonds provide?
options: It could be favorable - if VND weakens, the converted value of USD assets rises, and this benefit disappears entirely the moment the bond is denominated in a third currency
Only favorable if holding physical USD cash, not applicable to bonds
No benefit at all, so every foreign-currency asset should be avoided
USD bonds pay low interest, so they aren't worth considering
quiz.explanation: Currency risk can be a double-edged sword: if the bond's currency strengthens against your home currency, you gain on top of the coupon rate. This is also why some investors deliberately hold foreign-currency assets as a way to diversify and hedge against their home currency weakening.

quiz.question: You buy a USD bond paying 5%/year. After one year, VND strengthens 8% against USD. What's your actual result?
options: Exactly 5% profit as promised, since the coupon is paid in unchanged USD
About a 3% loss once converted to VND, even though the bond paid full interest, and this only holds once transaction costs on the currency conversion are ignored entirely
About 13% profit, since the coupon plus the exchange-rate move both add up
Can't be determined without knowing who issued the bond
quiz.explanation: Your actual return is measured in the currency you spend, not the currency the bond is denominated in. A 5% coupon plus a negative 8% exchange-rate move comes out to roughly negative 3%. This is a third layer of risk, separate from credit risk and interest rate risk.

quiz.question: How can an investor eliminate currency risk when buying foreign-currency bonds?
options: Wait until the exchange rate returns to the level at purchase before selling the bond
Only buy bonds issued by governments with an AAA credit rating
Use a currency-hedging contract, in exchange for paying a cost
There's no way; currency risk simply must be accepted, a factor that changes the calculation meaningfully
quiz.explanation: A forward or option contract can lock in a conversion rate, but the hedging cost usually eats up almost exactly the interest-rate gap between the two currencies - that's not a coincidence, but a consequence of the no-risk-free-arbitrage principle in markets.

quiz.question: Why does a US government bond still carry risk for a Vietnamese investor even though the US can virtually never default?
options: Because US bonds always pay less than Vietnam's inflation rate every year, a distinction worth checking before relying on it
Because the US government doesn't allow foreign investors to hold its bonds
Because zero credit risk doesn't erase currency risk and interest rate risk
Because foreign investors must pay a 50% tax on all coupon interest received
quiz.explanation: Safety in repayment is only one of three layers of risk. You can still lose money if the USD weakens against VND, or if US rates rise and you have to sell early - both entirely independent of whether the US can repay its debt.

quiz.question: Why do some investors still deliberately hold foreign-currency assets despite knowing about currency risk?
options: Because banks commit to compensating customers for any exchange-rate gap
Because foreign-currency assets are fully exempt from personal income tax in Vietnam, a benefit that in practice only materializes once income and spending are already diversified
Because the exchange rate always moves in one direction, so the real risk is zero
Because it's a way to spread risk when most of their assets are already in one currency
quiz.explanation: If all of your assets, income, and spending are in VND, you're effectively betting everything on one currency - even if you don't think of it as a bet. Holding some foreign-currency assets is a way to reduce that concentration risk, not to chase currency gains.

keyTakeaways: Investing in foreign-currency bonds adds one more layer of risk beyond credit risk and interest rate risk: exchange-rate risk
The actual return converted to your home currency depends on both the coupon rate and the exchange-rate move - the two can compound favorably or cancel each other out
Even a bond considered the safest in the world on a credit basis (like US government bonds) can still deliver a net loss to a foreign investor if the exchange rate moves unfavorably enough

practicePrompt.question: You believe VND will weaken 8% against USD over the coming year. You're choosing between a Vietnamese government bond (6%/year in VND) and a US government bond (4%/year in USD). In terms of return converted to VND, which choice is more favorable if your exchange-rate prediction is correct?
options: The US bond: 4% interest plus roughly an 8% conversion gain from VND weakening, well above 6%
The Vietnamese bond, because a 6%/year coupon is always higher than 4%/year regardless of how the exchange rate moves
Both deliver the same return once converted to VND, since the exchange rate doesn't affect bond yields
It's impossible to determine which is more favorable without knowing the exact face value of each bond
practicePrompt.explanation: If the exchange-rate prediction is correct, the 4% interest plus the roughly 8% conversion gain from VND weakening compound together, far exceeding the Vietnamese bond's 6%/year.

sections.text: If you're already comfortable with domestic bonds, international bonds open up more diversification opportunities - but they also bring an entirely new kind of risk that VND bonds don't have: currency risk.

An international bond is simply a bond issued in a foreign currency (usually USD, EUR, JPY) by a foreign government or multinational corporation. The most common example is the US Treasury Bond - considered one of the safest assets in the world on a credit basis, since the US Government can virtually never default on USD debt.
Why 'safe on credit' doesn't mean 'no risk'

This is the most confusing point. When a Vietnamese investor buys a US government bond, they receive interest and principal in USD. But ultimately they live and spend in VND, so at some point they need to convert that USD back into VND. If, during the holding period, VND strengthens against USD (meaning 1 USD buys fewer VND than before), then upon conversion, the value of the investment measured in VND falls, and can fall by more than the coupon interest received - leading to a net loss even though the bond itself was never at risk of default.

sections.label: A simple illustration
sections.text: You convert 235 million VND into 10,000 USD (at a rate of 23,500) to buy a US bond paying 4%/year. A year later, you receive 10,400 USD (principal + interest). If the rate at that point is 24,500 (USD has strengthened against VND), you convert back to 254.8 million VND - a gain of about 8.4% in VND terms, higher than the original coupon rate. But if the rate falls to 22,500 (USD has weakened), you only convert back to 234 million VND - less than your original capital, even though you received the full 4% coupon.

items: Currency risk is a double-edged sword: it can amplify returns if the exchange rate moves favorably, or wipe out returns (even causing a loss) if it moves unfavorably
This risk is entirely independent of the bond's credit quality - a US government bond remains absolutely safe on repayment ability, but is not absolutely safe on converted value
Some investors deliberately use foreign-currency assets (including international bonds) as a diversification tool, hedging against their home currency weakening over the long run

sections.text: For a beginner individual investor in Vietnam, international bonds usually aren't a top priority, since they require an international brokerage account, an understanding of exchange rates, and often a higher minimum capital threshold. But understanding currency risk is important knowledge if you later want to diversify your portfolio beyond Vietnam's borders.

lines: International bonds carry one more layer of risk independent of credit quality: exchange-rate risk.
Safety in repayment ability doesn't mean safety in converted value - worth remembering before investing abroad.
